content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper analyzes the problem of mode collapse in Imitation Learning from Observations. They show that this occurs under certain conditions (e.g. deterministic experts and bad network initializations). The authors propose a solution to this problem by way of data clustering and generative model pre-training.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- Highlighting the mode-collapse phenomenon is a really nice contribution. I wasn’t aware of it and I’m sure others in the community will appreciate learning about it.
- The empirical evidence for the mode collapse problem seems strong. Showing that the reward is low because of low policy entropy is nice.

Weaknesses:

- “While ILPO is extremely data efficient” - please clarify this sentence. Compared to what? Certainly not more data efficient than modern BC methods (IBC, etc) where the expert actions are known (albeit for a problem with different assumptions). It still suffers from the data complexity required to train the forward dynamics model when mapping the latent dynamics to the true state space (i.e. you need enough state coverage for this mapping to generalize over states at inference time). It’s certainly true that it’s more efficient than some methods, but the wording as-is seems underspecified.
- ILfO tends to struggle on real-world problems with significant visual complexity (and where state is partially observable). To this end, the paper would be significantly stronger with real-world results rather than toy simulation environments.
- The proposed solution to mode collapse seems nice (albeit a bit obvious) however I wonder if it scales to high dimensional action spaces where the mapping of actions to state transitions don’t necessarily collapse to a small number of “similar” actions. Perhaps the authors can speak to this in their rebuttal or show empirical results for high dimensional (non-simulated!) control problems?
- Can the authors discuss the robustness of the piecewise dynamics assumption? Under what practical settings is this invalid and how does this impact the proposed solution? Without thinking about it too much, this assumption does seem too strong to me.
- <strong personal opinion that doesn’t impact my assessment but worth mentioning> I think ILfO is a pretty niche area of even the supervised policy learning community, which is already pretty niche. IMO ILfO hasn’t been shown to work well when there is a large embodiment gap (e.g. the expert and policy have vastly different embodiments / degrees of freedom), and in the setting where the parameterization of the expert and policy are the same, it’s hard to come up with practical scenarios where you can’t explicitly infer or log the expert actions (the opposite is claimed in section 2, but I really disagree with this). The authors (in the intro and abstract) definitely use language to suggest that availability of expert actions is an issue that needs addressing (e.g. (3) in 2nd intro paragraph), however I’m not convinced this is uniformly accepted by everyone in the community. I would consider softening some of this language.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There are no issues of clarity that I can tell. The paper is easy to read and quite easy to understand. The experiments seem well carried out (with multiple seeds and std given) and there are sufficient comparisons against reasonable baselines. The paper would be totally reproducible if the authors release code (since all experiments are in simulation) - and I suggest the authors do this.

Likewise, this is the first paper I’ve read that discusses the issue of mode collapse, let alone proposing a solution, so I think there’s ample novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I’m torn on this paper. I really appreciate that the authors have highlighted and adequately explained the root cause of a very concrete problem with an existing method. However, the experimental results use pretty simple simulation environments that IMO don’t meet the bar for robust and compelling experimentation in 2022. This is particularly problematic given the known failure cases of this class of methods on more complex real-world environments (e.g. with complex visual observations).

While I do think this paper will be of interest to folks in the LFO community, I don’t think that this is a huge audience. However, I’m not sure how to factor in “nicheness” of the problem domain so I won't let that influence my final score.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors discover the mode collapse issue in Imitation Latent Polices from Observations. I.e., when training the forward dynamics model $G$, it is possible for the latent action set $Z$ to collapse to only one mode due to the bad initialization. They analyze this issue theoretically and experimentally. Then, under the piecewise continuous dynamics assumption, they propose to use agglomerative clustering to generate a better latent action set and then pretrain the forward dynamic model and latent policy model. They demonstrate the method in several environments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The authors find an interesting problem, and the proposed method is well motivated by some experimental evidence. The problem is alleviated to some extent by their solution.

Weakness:
1. The whole paper is not well organized. For example, the authors mix the methodology and experiment results in a single section, which makes the paper pretty messy and will confuse the readers. I think the writing of this paper is far from the standard of ICLR.
2. The piecewise continuous dynamics assumption is too strong. I suspect such a strong assumption will make it hard to apply the proposed method to some more complex scenarios. Especially, in the last sentence of Section4.3, the authors find that the pre-trained latent policy is sufficient to achieve good performance in some environments. So I suspect that the reason why this method works is that it takes advantage of the characteristics of the environments, not because it solves the mode collapse problem.
3. The proposed solution is trivial. Under the piecewise continuous dynamics assumption, using clustering to get a better initialization for latent actions is not novel.
4. The experiment design is too simple. The authors only demonstrate their method in some toy environments, e.g., MountainCar, LunarLander and Acrobot, etc. And they do not compare with any baseline methods. Since there have been many solutions proposed for mode collapse, it is necessary to compare with them.

Minor issues:
1. In Eq.(4), $\pi_{\omega}(z|s)$ --> $\pi_{\omega}(z|s_{t})$
2. In the last sentence of page 2, $\Delta_{z}$ --> $\Delta_{t}$
3. At the top of page 5, where is Figure 3?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is not clear and the proposed method is not very novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, the writing of this paper is poor, so it is necessary to revise the whole paper. Then there are some questions about the assumption and novelty. Please refer to the *Strength And Weaknesses part.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a method for imitation from observations only (ILfO), pointing out a problem analogous to mode collapse in generative models. They propose to solve this by a preprocessing step where the transitions are first clustered before training a dynamics/policy model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

+ The method is written up very clearly, and the in-depth dive into the clustering dynamics of the different environments was very interesting.
+ Empirically, the method does appear to help in some cases. 

Weaknesses

+ There is little formal motivation behind the overall clustering-based approach. The paper could be made much stronger with some more formal discussion of how the assumption of piecewise continuous dynamics gives the clustering-based method extra power. At its core, it seems like the ILfO problem is nonidentifiable: given a state $s_t$ which transitions to $s_{t+1}$ with probability 50% and $s'_{t+1}$ with probability 50%, it's impossible to say if this is due to deterministic dynamics and the agent having a random policy, or the agent having a deterministic policy and the dynamics being stochastic. Therefore there must be an inductive bias injected into the setting, and it's not clear what inductive bias the method actually has.
+ The approach is relatively rudimentary, with a (linear) PCA and simple agglomerative clustering. It's not clear if the method would scale to higher dimensional states, observations or actions. Similarly, several works examine the problem of finding the correct number of latent clusters, with Deep Dirichlet Process Models being one approach. It would also make sense to me to train a demonstrator which is explicitly encouraged to be random, such as a method trained with MaxEnt RL (e.g. SAC). 
+ The paper is light on details in several places. For instance, how is the agglomerative clustering carried out? Is there any featurization applied?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity

The paper is clear.

Quality

The work is of reasonable quality. However, it could be improved substantially. 

Novelty

As far as I know, the work is more or less novel.

Reproduciblity

Reproducibility seems limited due to a lack of detailed description of how the algorithm works.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Reject

The paper is a nice investigation of a method to improve imitation learning from demonstrations. However, there is little to no formal examination of the particular approach identified. Furthermore, the experimental settings are quite rudimentary (linear PCA, etc), and the method does not do well on certain cases. It's not clear if the method would scale to higher-dimensional settings.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors build upon ILPO, which is an ILfO (imitation learning from observations) method. ILPO learns a latent policy and transition model to explain the observations in the data and, in a second step, maps the latent (discrete) actions to real actions based on few labelled examples.

The authors note that ILPO can exhibit mode collapse: especially when there is no stochasticity in the expert policy, individual actions cannot be disentangled in latent space. To remidy this, they propose to pre-train the latent transition model and the policy. The key assumption is that similar transitions are caused by similar actions, allowing unsupervised clustering and labelling of transitions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strenghts

* The problem to be solved is well motivated.
* The proposed algorithm is also well motivated and evaluated, by running various ablations and plotting insightful figures (e.g. the PCA plots or rank correlation tables).
* Limits to the algorithm are also well highlighted and discussed (section 4.4) 

# Weaknesses

My main concern is with the overall level of quality of the presentation of the paper, which sometimes inhibits clarity. The paper is not badly written by any means and, in my opinion, not too far away from publication quality, but more work is required. To give some examples, which, by itself, do not seem much, but they add up overall and make reading unnecessarily confusing - to the point where I'm not sure I fully understand everything the authors are doing. 

* Figure 1 is quite central to a lot of the discussion, but the legend, in particular of (a) and (d) is not easy to read. E.g. There are four dahsed lines simply labelled as "Expert", with very different performances. I assume that one should infer whether they are deterministic or stochastic from the color of the solids lines - but even then this does not explain the difference in performance between the green and blue dashed line which both should correspond to a deterministic expert. (As an additional nit: I would find it helpful to spell out "Expert" and not shorten it to "Exp."
* Several figures use the title "PCA of something and actions", but I believe what is being meant is that it's the "PCA of something" with actions used for colouring.
* I did not understand at all how the rank correlations in Table 1 were computed (first paragraph in 4.3). Is the rank computed on _differences_ between states and transitions? I guess that makes sense for states, but why pairwise distances on transitions? (My reading of "containing the pair-wise distance of all states and transitions" is that the "pair-wise distances" also refers to transitions). Also, it is mentioned previously that ILPO assumes a discrete action space. However, here we are also computing distances of actions - which don't make sense for discrete actions. My guess is that _discretized_ actions are used, but there is an underlying continuous action space in which the distance makes sense?
* A bigger issue for me with this table is that it is used to justify that "similar transitions are usually caused by similar actions of the expert". However, one could imagine a world in which transitions are correlated to states and states correlated to actions through the expert - in which case we would see a correlation between transitions and actions, but the state still fully determines both the $z^l$ as well as the next state - so pertaining shouldn't help. I think one could disentange whether the transition-action correlation comes through the correlation with the states or not - and the authors even plot the state-action correlation - but the discussion of this is entirely missing. 
* Minor point: 4.3, second paragraph. The authors say they train end-to-end, but IMO what alg 1 is describing isn't really e2e training since they inject the unsupervised labelled $z$.
* I believe the fact that the imitation agent can outperform the expert in some of their experiments should be investigated further - it's not clear to me why this is the case. In particular, while this apparent mismatch of trained agent vs. expert is clearly an advantage in Mountain Car, I wonder whether it could be a disadvantage somewhere else.
* Section 4.4: If the results are not representative because you are using the wrong expert, why not use the right one?
* [nitpick] the caption of Fig 1 (appendix) is "Caption". It also shouldn't be numerated as Fig 1, but A1?

Apologies for appearing nitpicky. I believe this is a good and interesting paper, but, in my opinion, there is currently too much vagueness and lack of clarity in the presentation for acceptance. Furthermore, I believe some results require further investigation and explanation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
See above for details. The paper is generally well written, but with some sections not providing enough details.
The proposed algorithm is, to the best of my knowledge, novel. In terms of significance, the paper is currently presented as an improvement to a particular algorithm in ILfO, and hence of somewhat limited scope for impact.
However, some insights about problems in ILfO are, I believe, more general - which might be an interesting topic to be explored in a paragraph or two (though not necessary).

content.title: Preventing Mode Collapse When Imitating Latent Policies from Observations
content.abstract: Imitation from observations only (ILfO) is an extension of the classic imitation learning setting to cases where expert observations are easy to obtain but no expert actions are available. Most existing ILfO methods either require access to task-specific cost functions or large amounts of interactions with the target environment. Learning a forward dynamics model in combination with a latent policy has been shown to solve these issues. However, the limited supervision in the ILfO scenario can lead to a mode collapse in learning the generative forward model and the corresponding latent policy. In this paper, we analyse the mode collapse problem and show that it can occur whenever the expert is deterministic, and may also occur due to bad initialization of the models. Under the assumption of piecewise continuous system dynamics, we propose a method to prevent the mode collapse using clustering of expert transitions to pre-train the generative model and the latent policy. We show that the resulting method prevents mode collapse and improves performance in five different OpenAI Gym environments.
